newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN offers plan to repatriate 1.6 million Rwandans.
newsitem.headline: UN offers plan to repatriate 1.6 million Rwandans.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Tuesday it had presented a plan to gradually close down Rwandan refugee camps in Zaire and Tanzania to provoke mass repatriation of 1.6 million Rwandans living in the two states.
By giving Rwandan refugees a choice between voluntarily going home with U.N. help or relocating in countries of asylum, it said it hoped to break extremists' control over the teeming camps in Zaire.

The step-by-step plan is being circulated by Sadako Ogata, High Commissioner for Refugees who heads the agency, at a policy-setting meeting which opened in Geneva on Monday, UNHCR spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume told a news briefing.
Neither the timetable nor any other details were released.
"A package is being discussed, based on deteriorating conditions in Zaire and conditions which have improved in Rwanda. Leadership in the Zairean camps is very extreme," Berthiaume said.
"Camps would be closed and consolidated in a gradual and selective way," she added, declining to give details.
"Refugees would be given the possibility of repatriating or relocating. This would result in the extremist leaders exerting less control over the camp and humanitarian assistance."
Kamanda Wa Kamanda, Zaire's Interior Minister, was due to address the closed door annual meeting of UNHCR's 51-member executive committee, according to diplomats.

They said he was expected to reiterate a threat by Foreign Minister Kititwa Tumansi before the U.N. General Assembly in New York last week that Zaire would expel Rwandan and Burundi refugees if they did not return home voluntarily.
The UNHCR proposals coincide with a standstill in repatriation of Rwandans and a chronic shortage of funds.

But it was not clear how the gradual closure of the camps would be implemented or policed in Zaire, where Hutu hardliners intimidate the refugees, forcing them to stay. The hardliners have made clear they hope to regain power in Rwanda.
UNHCR has recommended that Zaire's security contingent in the camps be increased by 1,500 men, according to a U.N. source.

The refugees, mainly Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates, form one of UNHCR's biggest caseloads worldwide. There are some 1.1 million in Zaire.

Ogata was discussing the problem with officials from all countries of the Great Lakes region -- which also includes Burundi and Uganda -- as well as donor countries attending the executive committee, Berthiaume said.

Under UNHCR's proposal, Rwanda would pledge to promote returns and prevent hostile broadcasts against the former refugees. It would also be asked to reduce numbers held in its overflowing prisons and keep arrests to a minimum.

Refugees refusing to go home would be screened. If suspected of involvement in the 1994 massacres, they would be sent for questioning in coordination with the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, based in Arusha, Tanzania.

The Geneva-based agency has already been forced cut back its humanitarian programmes to the refugees due to a shortfall in contributions from donor countries. So far this year it has received just $199.6 million for its $253 million programme.
During 1996, fewer than 15,000 of those Rwandans who had fled in 1994 returned home from Zaire and Tanzania.
